## Results

Synthesis and characterizations of LiCl@Ni2Cl2(BTDD)
The composite adsorbent LiCl@Ni2Cl2(BTDD)_x (x=10/20/30/40, representing different LiCl solutions) was prepared using a scalable impregnation method in different mass concentrations (wt%) of LiCl solution at room temperature (see “Methods” section for preparation of Ni2Cl2(BTDD) and LiCl@Ni2Cl2(BTDD)). This approach requires neither pressurization nor ultra-high-temperature operations, with mild reaction conditions enabling effortless large-scale material preparation. Notably, the formulation of 30 wt% LiCl solution, i.e., LiCl@Ni2Cl2(BTDD)_30 was chosen for the key structural characteristics and the final device (Supplementary Figs. 3–5), because it enables a synergistic balance of the high water adsorption capacity and fast adsorption kinetics (details see the section “MOF-composite with varying LiCl solution concentrations” in the Supplementary Information).

Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analyses collectively indicated the successful loading of LiCl within the internal pore channels of the MOF material via the impregnation method (Supplementary Figs. 6–7). N2 adsorption isotherms of Ni2Cl2(BTDD) at 77 K (Fig. 1c) demonstrated that the pore volume (1.18 cm3 g–1) and Brunauer‒Emmett‒Teller (BET) surface area of 1839 m2 g–1 (Supplementary Fig. 8), close to the literature reference38. Furthermore, a sharp pore size distribution centered at 2.20 nm for Ni2Cl2(BTDD) (Fig. 1a, c) aligns well with the value reported in the literature38. As a contrast, LiCl@Ni2Cl2(BTDD)_30 showed a significantly lower pore volume (0.35 cm3 g–1) and BET surface area (504 m2 g–1, Supplementary Fig. 8), which may be due to the occupation of LiCl in the pores. Furthermore, the composite material shows a broader distribution centered at approximately 1.66 nm (Fig. 1c). This significant reduction in pore diameter by about 0.54 nm indicated the formation of a monolayer of LiCl on the internal pore surface (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 2). In addition, inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES) indicated that the LiCl to Ni2Cl2(BTDD) molar ratio is approximately 14:1 (Supplementary Table 2), and the distribution of LiCl in MOF pores was confirmed by time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) for LiCl@Ni2Cl2(BTDD)_30 (Supplementary Fig. 9).

Furthermore, the water sorption isotherms of LiCl@Ni2Cl2(BTDD)_30 composite sorbent show a distinctive three-step adsorption behavior (Fig. 1d), including salt chemisorption, deliquescence, and solution absorption at different water vapor pressures39. Notably, the material exhibited exceptionally high adsorption capacities under high-humidity conditions, with high water uptake reaching 3.46 g g‒1 at 30 °C and 80% RH, and 1.72 g g‒1 at 30 °C and 50% RH. Such high water uptake should be attributed to the deliquescence of LiCl29–31. To further investigate the desorption performance of the material, we systematically evaluated the desorption behavior at different temperatures (Fig. 1e). The results showed that the developed sorbent can achieve 94.7% desorption of the water uptake at temperatures as low as 60 °C (Supplementary Fig. 10). Subsequently, multi-cycle performance and stability tests showed that the adsorbent maintained a water vapor uptake consistently exceeding 3 g g‒1 over 10 cycles (as shown in Fig. 1f).

Construction of a modular photothermal-driven AWH system
Considering the application scenarios of solar-driven AWH, this adsorbent material exhibits significant advantages, particularly in arid regions, relative humidity at nighttime can exceed 50% even in dry environments, posing higher requirements for adsorbents to fully utilize long humidity windows of 8‒10 h duration daily (Supplementary Fig. 11, detailed climatic data analysis, please refer to the section: “Climatic data of typical arid and semi-arid regions” in Supplementary Information). While advanced adsorbents are crucial for AWH performance, their potential can only be fully realized through coordinated device-level optimization. Solar-driven AWH system works by alternating between nighttime vapor adsorption and daytime desorption, leveraging the natural day-night cycle. The daytime operation of AWH, which integrates sorbent desorption and vapor condensation, presents a fundamental thermal dilemma: desorption is favored at high temperatures, whereas condensation requires a cold surface (Fig. 2a, for a detailed thermodynamic AWH analysis, please see Supplementary Fig. 12 in the section on Device design and thermal management strategies in Supplementary Information). Driven by this critical insight into the process’s thermal demands, we engineered a highly compact and modular AWH system specifically to decouple these different temperature requirements. This system features a modular design, where the entire panel is composed of 4 cm × 4 cm adsorbent modules (Fig. 2b), and the detailed design drawings are provided in Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14. Such modularity enables flexible adaptation to diverse practical needs and facilitates system scalability for expanded applications. The device mainly consists of two core components: an integrated solar-thermal driven adsorption bed and a thermally enhanced condenser with dual-layer insulated mass transfer plates. Dual-layer insulated mass transfer plates (Fig. 2c) achieve thermal demand decoupling between condensation and desorption through internal thermal partitioning, which can effectively isolate thermal radiation and weaken convection.

We conducted laboratory performance tests in the climate chamber (water yield data as shown in Fig. 2d). Experimental results showed that under the system’s operating conditions, the increased water vapor desorption induced a sweating cooling effect. This phenomenon manifested as a temperature drop of over 10 °C (83.6 vs. 97.9 °C in Fig. 2e) on the photothermal panel through the cooling output generated by the adsorbent desorption process. These findings indicate that compared to Ni2Cl2(BTDD)-based device, MOF-composite possesses lower desorption temperatures and greater working capacity. Within 7 h, the device produced more than 1 L of liquid water per square meter in total (Fig. 2d), and the thermal efficiency increased by 25% compared with that before the salt composite. Based on this strategy, the proposed device achieves an ultrahigh volumetric water harvesting capacity of 30.3 L m‒3, ranking among the highest levels reported to date for existing diurnal solar energy-driven AWH devices9,10,15,32,40–43 (for a detailed device performance comparison, please see Supplementary Table 2).

In addition, the working conditions adopted in the experiment were the light intensity equivalent to noon sunlight commonly used in existing literature. However, considering the variation of daytime irradiation, such continuous high-intensity irradiation conditions do not last for 7 h. Therefore, the adsorbent must adapt to a lower desorption temperature to meet the actual needs. According to our analysis, the composite strategy we proposed can achieve high-performance desorption at a lower desorption temperature through simple salt hygroscopic factor compounding. Tests under varying irradiation and humidity conditions demonstrate that the device equipped with the developed MOF-composite achieves strong performance across a wider range of climatic conditions (Supplementary Fig. 15 and Supplementary Table 3 shown in Supplementary Information, section on “Performance of the proposed AWH system under different operating conditions”). Notably, it produced a high water yield exceeding 500 g m‒2 even under a low irradiation intensity of just 400 W m‒2. The system developed based on this strategy thus has greater practical application value. We conducted multi-cycle tests at the device level to verify the stability of the combination for the material and system (Fig. 2f). The results of 12-cycle tests at the device level showed that the system could operate stably under the test conditions. During the laboratory cycling tests, the proposed device consistently achieved a water production yield of approximately 42 g, while maintaining a water vapor recovery rate above 90% (see the section of “Multiple cycling performance tests” in Supplementary Information), indicating that the system is capable of stable operation.

Comparative field testing across different climatic regions
To better evaluate the performance of the constructed system in different real-world application scenarios, we conducted field experiments under various climatic conditions in Shanghai (31.0271° N, 121.4460° E), Jinan (36.6599° N, 117.2334° E), and Kunming (24.8644° N, 102.8586° E). During each experiment, all test conditions (including pure powder and composite adsorbent systems) were kept identical, and no auxiliary equipment was used, as shown in Fig. 3a. All tests were performed under consistent protocols; both the MOF-composite and Ni2Cl2(BTDD) systems were evaluated in parallel without any auxiliary equipment.

Outdoor experiments demonstrated that the MOF-composite system consistently outperformed the pure MOF device under varied climatic conditions (Table 1). In Shanghai and Jinan, representing moderate-to-high humidity environments, the composite system collected nearly 50% more water, with the most enhancement observed in Jinan (over 90% increase in water yield). Even under the low-temperature winter conditions of Kunming, the MOF-composite system still achieved effective water production, confirming its broad applicability.

A detailed analysis of site-specific performance revealed several key advantages of the proposed MOF-composite material. In Shanghai, the experiment lasted three days (temperature data of the tests on October 3 is shown in Fig. 3b), with no electrical auxiliary equipment used throughout the process. The final experimental results demonstrate that the proposed device with MOF-composite exhibits superior adaptability to daily cycling operations. Under the conditions of a daily maximum solar irradiance of 0.8 sun and an ambient temperature of 33 °C, the maximum driving heat source temperature provided by the photothermal plate is approximately 85 °C, and the duration during which the temperature exceeds 80 °C throughout the day is about 5 h (Fig. 3b). Experimental observations showed that liquid water could appear in the water collection bottle around 9:30 a.m., 1 h earlier than the Ni2Cl2(BTDD)-based device, which started to produce water around 10:30 a.m. This indicates that the device improved by the composite material strategy can achieve desorption under lower-RH environmental conditions. Meanwhile, we observed the same phenomenon as in laboratory experiments: the composite adsorbent exhibits higher water vapor desorption capacity, thereby providing greater cooling capacity for photothermal components. Compared to the MOF-based device, the solar thermal panel with MOF-composite demonstrated a temperature reduction effect of approximately 10 °C during testing.

It also extended the effective adsorption period, fully utilizing the high nighttime humidity and achieving continuous moisture capture (Fig. 3d). Different from the Ni2Cl2(BTDD)-based device, which reaches adsorption saturation around 11 p.m. at lower water uptake, the proposed device with MOF-composite fully utilizes the high-humidity environment at night, thereby achieving the ability of potential continuous adsorption at night. Compared to the Ni2Cl2(BTDD)-based device, the device with MOF-composite achieves ~46% higher water vapor adsorption and desorption capacity (detailed data and analysis can be found in Supplementary Information, section of “Outdoor experimental details” in Shanghai) while realizing precise mass matching between adsorption and desorption phases, thereby enabling stable water production from 30.2 to 32.6 g day‒1. Furthermore, outdoor testing results confirmed the operational stability of the proposed device with the MOF-composite. These comparisons also demonstrate that utilizing the composite adsorbent’s characteristics of low desorption temperature and high adsorption capacity enables adaptation to variations in operating conditions through both desorption and adsorption pathways, thereby effectively enhancing system efficiency. To verify the reliability of field data, we further replicated Shanghai’s stable noon conditions during the second day in the climatic chamber, which confirmed consistent temperature trends and performance metrics between indoor and outdoor settings (Supplementary Fig. 17).

The experimental results have been further validated in different climatic regions, as exemplified by Jinan and Kunming (Supplementary Fig. 18). In Jinan, despite lower ambient and photothermal temperatures (~10 °C below that in Shanghai as shown in Supplementary Fig. 18a), the composite device nearly doubled the water yield of the pure MOF system, highlighting its superior performance under suboptimal solar irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 18b). In Kunming during winter. The results demonstrated that the adsorption material achieved high-performance liquid water production at a driving temperature as low as 60 °C (Supplementary Fig. 18c, d), corresponding to a saturated vapor pressure only one-third of that at 85 °C (19.923 vs. 57.875 kPa). In previous studies, the required heat source temperature often exceeded 90 °C due to impaired heat and mass transfer during actual system formation13,15,18,35. Thus, this composite strategy can better enhance the applicability of AWH under conditions of low irradiation and heat source temperatures.

Collectively, the field tests validate that the MOF-composite significantly enhances solar-to-water generation across diverse climates. The solar-driven AWH system operates by utilizing low-grade solar thermal energy to desorb at a lower temperature, thereby achieving the transformation of water vapor into liquid water. Consequently, the improvement in water collection efficiency reflects an overall enhancement in energy efficiency. Specifically, the efficiency improvement reached 91% in Jinan under a continental climate, while an average enhancement of approximately 50% was achieved in medium-to-high humidity regions such as Shanghai and Jinan. These results collectively underscore the significant potential of synergizing MOF-derived composite sorbents with advanced thermal management in AWH devices.

Water quality analysis
The analysis of water quality indicates that, within the allowable precision range of testing instruments (details of testing instruments are introduced in Supplementary Information: Details of water ion concentration analysis), the ion concentration of the proposed water sample is identical to that of distilled water. No lithium ions or nickel ions were detected, confirming its suitability for direct consumption. This result demonstrates that the collected water originates entirely from the condensation of water vapor generated during the desorption process on the condenser walls (as shown in Table 2). Furthermore, it confirms the absence of salt leakage throughout the process.

## Methods

Synthesis of MOF
The synthesis of Ni2Cl2(BTDD) was according to the method in the literature19.

Synthesis of LiCl@Ni2Cl2(BTDD)
We initially synthesized the MOF material Ni2Cl2(BTDD) via a reflux synthesis method based on previously reported preparation protocols, followed by drying the obtained product. The dried MOF powder was then immersed in a 10/20/30/40 wt% LiCl (Anhydrous LiCl with AR≥99.0% was purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd.) solution for a 24-h impregnation treatment. Magnetic stirring was applied during the impregnation process to ensure sufficient penetration of the LiCl solution into the MOF pores. The resulting solution was then centrifuged at 1000 rpm (10,619×g) to achieve preliminary solid-liquid separation, with the material precipitating at the bottom of the centrifuge tubes. Centrifugation was performed for 10 min to ensure complete phase separation. The separated material was subsequently dried at 80 °C to obtain the final composite adsorbent LiCl@Ni2Cl2(BTDD). For ease of description, we named the MOF composite material immersed in a 10/20/30/40 wt% LiCl solution as LiCl@Ni2Cl2(BTDD)_10/20/30/40, respectively.

Design of AWH prototype
We constructed a branch biomimetic AWH device using inexpensive and reliable 304 stainless steel as the raw material. We have detailed the device’s design drawings and usage details in Supplementary Information: Design schematics of the AWH device and the insulated mass transfer plate.

Experimental details
We used an electronic recorder (TP1000 paperless recorder from SHENZHEN TOPRIE ELECTRONICS CO., LTD.) to record the temperature data during the process. In SI, we have also described some key experimental details and photos taken during the tests, and other experimental information can be provided upon request.

Data availability
The data supporting the findings of this study are available within the paper and its Supplementary Information files. Source data are available from the corresponding authors upon request.
